name: Battle of Badr
info: On 13 March 624 CE (17 Ramadan, 2 AH) Muhammad's followers from Medina defeated a larger Qurayshi army from Mecca near Badr, killing several Meccan leaders and strengthening Muhammad's position.

facts.place: Near the city of Badr, Medina Province, in present-day Saudi Arabia, in a valley between sand dunes and hills
facts.sides: Muhammad's army of 313 to 317 men (313 is the generally accepted figure, with two horses and 70 camels) against a Qurayshi army led by Amr ibn Hisham, given as around 1300 men with 100 horses in one passage and as nearly one thousand in another
facts.outcome: The Medinan army broke the Meccan lines; scholars estimate about 70 Meccan dead, 14 known Muslim dead and some 70 prisoners.

t: The fighting began over a Meccan caravan from the Levant, but the caravan escaped by another route and the two armies met at Badr anyway.
The only account of the battle is the Islamic tradition, written down some time later, and some histories doubt how much beyond it can be established.
Islamic tradition holds that angels took part and that the victory was divine; other sources attribute it to Muhammad's strategy.
dyk: The Qur'an calls the battle Yawm al-Furqan, 'The Day of the Criterion', and Ibn Ishaq's biography of Muhammad includes a complete name by name roster of the Muslim army.
ev: The Hijra: Muhammad and his followers migrate to Medina, where the community chooses him as leader
Early in the year Muhammad learns of a Meccan caravan returning from the Levant and gathers a force of around 300 men to intercept it
Abu Sufyan sends word to Mecca and changes the caravan's route; the Quraysh assemble an army
The Muslim army camps at the wells of Badr on 12 March, and the Quraysh march into the valley at midnight on 13 March
On 13 March the battle opens with duels and then a Meccan charge, and the Muslim counter-attack breaks the Meccan lines
About 70 prisoners are taken and, on Abu Bakr's advice, mostly released for ransom
Muhammad marches into Mecca, whose peaceful surrender Abu Sufyan helps to negotiate

sections.background:
After the Hijra, the migration to Medina in 622 CE, the people of Medina chose Muhammad as leader of the community, and his followers decided to raid the caravans of the Meccans as they passed by Medina. In early 624 a Qurayshi caravan led by Abu Sufyan ibn Harb was returning to Mecca from the Levant, possibly from Gaza, carrying merchandise worth 50,000 dinars and guarded by 70 men. It was unusually large, possibly because several smaller caravans had joined for safety, and all the leading Meccan financiers had a share in it.

Two reasons are given for Muhammad's decision to intercept it. The first was a policy of recovering wealth from the Quraysh, who had confiscated Muslims' properties in Mecca after the Hijra. The second was that a successful attack would impress the Meccans and might deter a future attack on Medina. Abu Sufyan sent word to Mecca asking for reinforcements. Traditional Muslim sources say his spies had told him of the Muslim plan, a view accepted by Tariq Ramadan. W. Montgomery Watt argues that since the Meccan army took a week to reach Badr, Abu Sufyan must have sent his request before the Muslim preparations began, as an astute man who anticipated an attack. A messenger, Damdam ibn Amr al-Ghifari, cried out the alarm at the Ka'bah, and Abu Sufyan rerouted the caravan toward the Red Sea and escaped.
sections.forces:
Muhammad gathered 313 to 317 men; sources vary, and 313 is the generally accepted number: 82 Muhajirun, 61 men of the Aws and 170 of the Khazraj. They were not well equipped, with two horses and 70 camels, so that one camel served two or three men in turn. The army had two divisions, the Muhajirun under a flag carried by Ali ibn Abi Talib and the Ansar under Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, with Zubayr commanding the right flank and Miqdad the left. At a council of war Abu Bakr, Umar and Miqdad spoke for fighting, and Muhammad wanted the view of the Ansar, who had not pledged at 'Aqabah to fight beyond their own territory. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh pledged their obedience, and the march continued.

The Quraysh assembled around 1300 men, 100 horses and many camels, though another passage of the same account puts it at nearly one thousand. At al-Juhfah a second message told them the caravan was safe. The Banu Zuhrah, around 300, turned back on al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq's advice, but Amr ibn Hisham insisted on going on to Badr and holding a feast there. The Quraysh brought no women and children, which suggests that they lacked time to prepare. Muhammad took the well nearest the Quraysh, on a suggestion from al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir, and had the others blocked or destroyed. A Meccan scout reported about 300 men keen to fight to the last.
sections.course:
The battle began with duels. Al-Aswad ibn Abd al-Asad swore to drink from the Muslims' well or destroy it, and Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib killed him. Utba ibn Rabi'a, his brother Shayba and his son al-Walid then came out, and the Meccans, who wanted to fight only the Muhajirun, rejected three Ansar. Ali killed al-Walid and Hamza killed Shayba. Ubayda ibn al-Harith, wounded, was carried back and died later of a disease. A shower of arrows followed, with several more duels, most won by the Muslims, and then the Meccans charged.

As they charged, Muhammad prayed, according to the tradition, “O Allah! Should this group (of Muslims) be defeated today, You will no longer be worshipped.” He then gave the order to counter-attack and threw a handful of pebbles at the Meccans, probably a traditional Arabian gesture, calling “Defaced be those faces!” The Muslims rushed the Qurayshi lines, and the Meccans, understrength and unenthusiastic about fighting, broke and ran. The battle lasted a few hours and was over by early afternoon. Muslims attribute the Meccans' fear to divine intervention: the Qur'an says in chapter 8, verse 12, that God inspired angels to strengthen the believers, and Muslim sources take the accounts of angels, including Jibreel, literally. Other sources credit Muhammad's strategy.
sections.aftermath:
Three days after the battle Muhammad left Badr for Medina. About 70 prisoners were taken, among them a number of Qurayshi leaders. Abu Bakr argued for ransoming them as kin, while Umar argued that they should all be executed, each by the relative closest to him, and Muhammad accepted Abu Bakr's view. The prisoners are noted to have been treated humanely, and William Muir records one saying that the Medinans made them ride while they walked. Most were released on payment of ransom, and literate prisoners could earn release by teaching ten persons to read and write. Earlier, some Muslims had beaten two captured Meccan water-bearers into giving false answers, and Muhammad later strongly condemned this.

Scholars estimate Meccan casualties at around 70, though only the more prominent names are known: Amr ibn Hisham, Umayya ibn Khalaf, Utba, Shayba, al-Walid ibn Utba and al-Aswad. Nadr ibn al-Harith and Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt were also killed, but the circumstances are unclear: some sources say they fell in the fighting and were buried in a pit, while Safiur Rahman al-Mubarakpuri writes that they were captured and executed by Ali. The names of the 14 Muslims who died of the fighting or its wounds are all known.
sections.sources:
All knowledge of the battle comes from traditional Islamic accounts, recorded and compiled some time after the event, such as those of the 8th century, together with the references to it in the Qur'an. Some histories find little evidence beside these, so that the historicity and authenticity of the battle are debatable. The accounts differ on numbers: the Muslim force is given as 313 to 317 men, and the Meccan army as around 1300 in one passage and nearly one thousand in another. Little is known of the Qurayshi army's progress from Mecca to Badr, and the Meccan side is known only through what the Muslim tradition reports of it.

Historians also differ over how Abu Sufyan learned of the plan. Traditional Muslim sources, and Tariq Ramadan, hold that his spies told him of the Muslim preparations; Watt argues that he must have sent his request for help before they began. Ibn Ishaq's biography of Muhammad includes a complete roster of the Muslim army, and many hadiths identify veterans of Badr as such, a sign of the battle's later standing. Several features of the account are told as what Muslims believe: the night's rain as a blessing for the believers, the army's refreshing sleep, and the angels, with Jibreel, who the Qur'an and hadith say took part. The same accounts are the source of the claim, found in Islamic history, that the victory was decisive and due to divine intervention.
sections.legacy:
Badr was the first large engagement between the Muslims and the Quraysh. It transformed Muhammad from an outcast of Mecca into the leader of a new community and city-state at Medina. Marshall Hodgson adds that it forced other Arabs to regard the Muslims as challengers and potential inheritors of Qurayshi prestige. Soon afterwards Muhammad expelled the Banu Qaynuqa, a Jewish tribe of Medina, said to be a penalty for assaulting a Muslim woman and breaking the peace treaty; the tribe is also described as a threat to his political position. His chief opponent in Medina, Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, was weakened.

Abu Sufyan, safe with the caravan, became chief of the Quraysh almost by default after the deaths of so many nobles, and later helped negotiate Mecca's peaceful surrender; his son Mu'awiya founded the Umayyad Caliphate. Hamza, who fought well at Badr, was killed by an assassin at Uhud. The last of the Badr veterans died during the First Fitna. In the Qur'an the battle is Yawm al-Furqan, and Muslim armies and organisations have named operations after it, among them Egypt's offensive in the 1973 war and Pakistan's actions in the 1999 Kargil War. It has appeared in films and television.

summary: At Badr in March 624 CE a Medinan army of about 313 under Muhammad defeated a larger Meccan force led by Amr ibn Hisham, killing several Qurayshi leaders. Islamic tradition holds the victory to be divinely aided; the battle is known almost entirely from later Islamic accounts.
notes: The article gives two Meccan strengths: 'nearly one-thousand' in the lead, 'around 1300' in the body. I gave both. It also says the Banu Zuhrah, around 300, turned back, and a scout reported 300 Muslims; I did not try to reconcile them.
The article calls Badr 'near the city of Badr, Medina Province': I gave the place as the article does. It does not give a modern distance from Medina.

The article's Muslim casualties section is empty beyond one line: the names of the 14 Muslims 'killed during the course of the war or later (due to injuries sustained during the war)' are all known. I wrote 'died of the fighting or its wounds', which may read the 'war' as the battle; the editor should check.

The sources section is partly my arrangement from the Legacy paragraph (all knowledge from traditional accounts; historicity debatable), the Ibn Ishaq roster and the Watt/Ramadan disagreement. The article names no 8th-century author except Ibn Ishaq.

Left out: the debate over Umar's and Abu Bakr's speeches in full, Miqdad's and Sa'd's quoted speeches, Muir's quotation, the references to Iblis and Suraqa, the Hubab episode details beyond the well, Uthman and Ruqayya, Salman, Hakim ibn Hizam, the Libyan 2011 anniversary, film titles.

The article's sentence on the Banu Qaynuqa gives its own reasons ('for assaulting a Muslim woman' and 'for breaking the peace treaty', 'threatened Muhammad's political position'); other sources may differ. Wording is the article's.
The article says Muhammad 'praised and supplicated for' Miqdad; omitted. No physical description of Muhammad is given or used.
